newsitem.title: GERMANY: Veba in no hurry to find telecoms partner.
newsitem.headline: Veba in no hurry to find telecoms partner.

text.p: German energy group Veba AG is taking its time about finding a new international partner for its telecommunications business and does not expect to present any prospects for at least another three months.

Veba chairman Ulrich Hartmann told reporters late on Tuesday that he regretted the recent departure of Cable and Wireless Plc from their partnership. The company would now focus on Germany, but still sought a foreign investor.
"I believe that we as newcomers to the business need a partner to provide know-how for international activities," Hartmann told a gathering of business journalists in Frankfurt.
"But I'm afraid I will have to disappoint anyone who thinks we are going to present a new partner in the next few weeks or even in the next three months. We are not in a hurry."

Cable and Wireless bailed out of its partnership with Veba just as the two were about to sign a final deal to bring utility RWE AG into the group following a reassesment of C&W's strategy after a change of managment.

Veba and RWE have set up a joint telecoms venture for the German market called Otelo, which will present a new business plan to the public at the Cebit information technology fair in Hanover next month.
Speculation arose last week that Veba was in talks with British Telecom after the German energy group confirmed last week that Hartmann met with BT chairman Ian Vallance.
"We are not in any form of talks about a partnership with British Telecom," Hartmann told Reuters after the press briefing. "That would not make any sense."

However, Hartmann added that he was talking "to a number of interested companies" in the United States, Europe and Asia and that he was looking for a firm that was "ready to make a considerable investment in Germany".
"A lot of companies come into question. Many have come forward," he said, declining to identify any companies or to say how far along talks were.

As Germany and the rest of Europe race toward January 1998, when most European Union members will erase the final barriers to full competition in the telecoms sector, Hartmann said Veba has taken a more realistic view as to what it can achieve.

Its alliance with RWE is just one of several gearing up to challenge incumbent monopoly Deutsche Telekom for a piece of Europe's biggest telecoms market, expected to be worth more than 100 billion marks ($60 billion) in the year 2000.
Hartmann said the company would no longer try to get involved in "peripheral businesses" such as digital pay television, but would focus on core telecoms activities.
"Mobile communications and basic telecommunications are now at the centre of our activities," he said.

Veba owns around 30 percent of the mobile phone group E-Plus Mobilfunk GmbH. Hartmann reiterated his interest in buying out the 30 percent E-Plus stake held by steel group Thyssen AG, but seemed doubtful this would happen.

"We have never made a secret of the fact that we would like to buy Thyssen's stake in E-Plus," he said. "The talks have always failed over large differences in price considerations and I cannot see this changing in the foreseeable future."
Hartmann added that the stake could also go to RWE and that it would be brought into their joint telecoms venture.
"It really doesn't matter at all whether we buy it or RWE buys it, because it will be brought into Otelo, just as we have put our E-Plus stake in Otelo," he said. ($ = 1.703 German Marks)
